THE VANISHING DARK
How artificial light at night is reshaping the natural world

A  For most of the Earth's history, the planet followed a reliable rhythm of daylight and darkness. Plants, animals and humans evolved under this cycle, and many species came to **rely on** darkness as much as on light. Over the past 150 years, however, that rhythm has been **disrupted** on an extraordinary scale. Street lamps, illuminated advertising and floodlit buildings now produce a glow that can be seen from space, and a 2019 survey by the Institute for Nocturnal Studies estimated that more than 80 per cent of the world's population lives under skies affected by artificial light. For astronomers, this so-called 'light pollution' has long been a source of frustration. **Only recently have** ecologists begun to treat it as a serious environmental threat.

B  Insects are among the most obvious victims. Anyone who has watched moths circling a porch light has seen the problem in miniature. Dr Helena Marsh, an entomologist at Northfield University, spent three summers counting insects around 40 street lamps in rural areas. She found that the lamps attracted insects from as far as 200 metres away, and that roughly one in three of them died before dawn, either from exhaustion or because they were eaten by predators that had learnt to hunt beneath the lights. 'A single street light may seem **insignificant**,' Marsh notes, 'but when you multiply it by millions, the **cumulative** effect on insect populations is enormous.' She believes the deaths she recorded may be only **the tip of the iceberg**. Since many insects pollinate crops and wild flowers, their decline could have **far-reaching consequences** for food production.

C  Birds face a different set of dangers, particularly **migratory** species. Many travel at night and **navigate** partly by the stars. Bright city lights can draw them off course, causing them to circle tall buildings until they become exhausted or collide with glass. In one incident in 2017, around 400 songbirds were found dead at the base of a single office tower after a night of low cloud. Light also affects birds that do not migrate. Research by the ornithologist Paolo Ferri found that blackbirds living near street lamps began singing up to five hours earlier than those in darker woodland, and laid their eggs nearly a month sooner. While this might appear harmless, early breeding can leave chicks hatching before enough food is available.

D  The effects are not limited to animals. Trees close to street lamps have been observed keeping their leaves several weeks longer in autumn, a change that may make them more **vulnerable to** frost damage. In humans, bright light late in the evening **suppresses** the production of melatonin, a hormone that controls sleep. Several studies have linked **exposure** to night-time light with poor sleep quality, although researchers stress that it is difficult to **separate** the effects of outdoor lighting **from** those of phones and television screens.

E  Not all scientists agree on how serious the problem is. Professor Alan Whitby, an urban ecologist, accepts that light pollution is a real issue but warns against **exaggerating** its importance. In his view, **habitat loss**, pesticide use and climate change remain far greater threats to wildlife, and attention should not be **diverted** away from them. He also points out that many studies have been carried out over short periods in small areas, which makes it hard to **draw firm conclusions** about long-term trends. Others reply that **the very fact that** light pollution is relatively easy to fix makes it worth addressing. 'Unlike climate change, this is a problem we could largely solve within a decade,' says Marsh.

F  Practical solutions already exist. One of the simplest is to **switch off** unnecessary lighting late at night, a measure that several towns in northern France have **adopted** since 2015. Another is to use shielded lamps that direct light downwards rather than allowing it to spill into the sky. The colour of light also matters: warm, amber lighting appears to attract far fewer insects than the bright white LEDs that many councils have installed in recent years to save energy. Ironically, the switch to LEDs, intended as an environmentally friendly policy, has in some places made the problem worse, because the lamps are cheaper to run and are therefore often left on for longer.

G  Public attitudes may prove to be the biggest **obstacle**. Many people associate bright streets with safety, and proposals to dim lighting are often **met with resistance**. Yet there is little evidence to support this belief. A five-year trial in 62 English towns found no significant rise in crime or road accidents where lights were dimmed or switched off after midnight. Supporters of darker skies hope that such findings, together with a growing appreciation of the night sky itself, will gradually **shift public opinion**. **As Marsh puts it**, 'We do not need to live in darkness. We simply need to use light more wisely.'
